text:
The hum died first. Then the lights surrendered, leaving the city a silhouette against a bruised, starless sky. On the rooftop garden, the silence was not empty but heavy, pressing against eardrums tuned to the usual symphony of traffic and HVAC units. Now, only the wind moved through the trellis, rustling dry leaves like whispered secrets.

I sat on the concrete ledge, legs dangling over the abyss of unlit streets below. The darkness here was absolute, stripping away the visual clutter of urban life. In its place, scent bloomed: damp earth, jasmine, the metallic tang of ozone from distant, failing grids. Time seemed to pool in the shadows, viscous and slow. A single moth, pale as bone, drifted past my knee, navigating by instinct rather than illumination. For that first hour, we were no longer consumers or commuters. We were merely breaths suspended in the void, waiting for the world to remember how to speak.
